node.label: Gregory S. Kealey
node.date_label: ‘The Honest Workingman’ 1976 · ‘The Working Class in Recent Canadian Historical Writing’ 1978 · Toronto Workers Respond to Industrial Capitalism 1980 · ‘Prospects in the 1980s’ 1981 · Dreaming of What Might Be (with Palmer) 1982 · ‘1919: The Canadian Labour Revolt’ 1984 · Class, Gender, and Region 1988 · RCMP Security Bulletins (with Whitaker) 1989–97 · Spying on Canadians 2017
node.description: A Canadian historian of the working class, and later of political policing, who argued for putting class at the centre of Canadian history. Of Toronto's craftsmen he wrote that 'Skilled workers in the nineteenth century exercised far more power than we have previously realized', amounting to 'a high degree of workers' control of production' (1976); in 1981 he held that 'it is now necessary to locate class conflict and class struggle at the centre of modern Canadian history', and he criticised the regional turn, under which 'Canadian historians have come to believe everything was different everywhere', as he had criticised the 'so-called "limited identities"' in 1978. David Brody, reviewing Toronto Workers Respond to Industrial Capitalism (1980), found it marked by 'what might be termed the Gutman school' and a useful foundation, but judged that Kealey had 'overreached himself' in its interpretation; Bettina Bradbury (1987) faulted him and Bryan Palmer for partially dismissing a Knights of Labor editor's picture of the ideal working-class wife as 'crude moralizing', and Joan Sangster (2000) found in both men's early books 'a proclivity to centre on skilled male workers and their actions in the public sphere'. From the late 1980s he edited the RCMP's security bulletins with Reg Whitaker and studied state surveillance of labour and the left, concluding that 'For the RCMP the Cold War began in 1919, not in 1946' (1992).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Gregory S. Kealey (b. 1948); with Russell Hann, Linda Kealey and Peter Warrian, Primary Sources in Canadian Working Class History, 1860–1930 (1973); “‘The Honest Workingman’ and Workers’ Control: The Experience of Toronto Skilled Workers, 1860–1892” (Labour/Le Travailleur, 1976); with Peter Warrian, eds., Essays in Canadian Working Class History (1976); “The Working Class in Recent Canadian Historical Writing” (Acadiensis, 1978); Toronto Workers Respond to Industrial Capitalism, 1867–1892 (1980); “Labour and Working-Class History in Canada: Prospects in the 1980s” (Labour/Le Travailleur, 1981); with Bryan D. Palmer, Dreaming of What Might Be: The Knights of Labor in Ontario, 1880–1900 (1982); “1919: The Canadian Labour Revolt” (Labour/Le Travail, 1984); “The Structure of Canadian Working-Class History” (1985); ed., Class, Gender, and Region: Essays in Canadian Historical Sociology (1988); with Reg Whitaker, eds., R.C.M.P. Security Bulletins (1989–97); “State Repression of Labour and the Left in Canada, 1914–20” (CHR, 1992); “The RCMP, the Special Branch, and the Early Days of the Communist Party of Canada” (Labour/Le Travail, 1992); Workers and Canadian History (1995). After 2000: with Lara Campbell and Dominique Clément, eds., Debating Dissent (2012); with Reg Whitaker and Andrew Parnaby, Secret Service (2012); Spying on Canadians (2017). Readings: Bercuson (1981); Brody (1981–82); McKay (1981–82); Bradbury (1987); Morton (2000); Sangster (2000).
node.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14, all in the journals' own PDFs unless stated: his 1976 Labour/Le Travailleur essay (pp. 32–34 and 58–62 read closely, the rest skimmed); his 1978 Acadiensis review essay (pp. 116–117 and 134–135, UNB Libraries PDF); his 1981 'Prospects in the 1980s' in full; '1919: The Canadian Labour Revolt' (1984), pp. 11–17 and 34 and the conclusion; his introduction to Class, Gender, and Region (1988), pp. 1–7, in the CCLH reprint on AU Press's site; and the opening of his 1992 RCMP documentary article (pp. 169–171). Reception read: Bercuson (1981), pp. 95–96; David Brody's review of Toronto Workers (Labour/Le Travailleur 8/9, 1981–82, pp. 361–364) in full; Ian McKay (1981–82), pp. 185–186, 214 and 219–224; Bettina Bradbury (1987), pp. 23–25 and 34–36; Desmond Morton (2000), pp. 11 and 22–27; Joan Sangster (2000), pp. 130 and 133; Careless's 1979 Jackson lecture (web text). Unread: the monographs Toronto Workers (1980) and Dreaming of What Might Be (1982), quoted only as Brody, Bradbury and Morton quote them; 'The Structure of Canadian Working-Class History' (1985), known through Bradbury's quotation; 'The writing of social history in English Canada, 1970–1984' (Social History, 1985); his 1992 Journal of Canadian Studies reply to Bliss (Project MUSE served a verification wall); the 1992 CHR and Intelligence and National Security articles, the Security Bulletins, Secret Service (2012) and Spying on Canadians (2017), cited at title and catalogue level; McNaught (1981) and Ramsay Cook's 'The Making of Canadian Working-Class History' (1983). He is not presented as a founder: Freeman (2002) names him with Palmer and Sangster in the founding generation of Labour/Le Travail; Morton (2000) calls him the group's 'undoubted inspirational leader'; in 1981 he stressed 'the collective nature of the work' and noted that the group's first collective statement was 'drafted by Russell Hann'. The 1981 essay is not a reply to Bercuson's essay in the same issue: both were first given at the McGill 'Class and Culture' conference in March 1980 (p. 68 n.), and Kealey answers Bercuson's 1979 charge of 'obeisance to E.P. Thompson'. Contested in period by Bercuson (1981), Brody (1981–82), McKay (1981–82, on the concept of culture), Bradbury (1987) and Sangster (2000) on gender, and Morton (2000). Post-2000 works are dated in labels and text.

proposed_edges.relationship: Workers' control and class at the centre: Toronto skilled workers' power on the job (1976) and their responses to industrial capitalism (1980), with a periodization by stages of capitalism and a case for class analysis and the materiality of culture (1978–81); contested by Bercuson and Brody (1981) and by feminist critics (1987–2000)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. '“The Honest Workingman” and Workers’ Control', Labour/Le Travailleur 1 (1976), pp. 32–68, read at pp. 32–34 and 58–62: 'Skilled workers in the nineteenth century exercised far more power than we have previously realized. … In Toronto work places, craftsmen employed their monopoly on skill and experience to dictate terms to their employers … which, in modern parlance, gave to these late nineteenth century craftsmen a high degree of workers' control of production' (p. 32); he draws on David Montgomery's 'veterans of industrial life' and on Raymond Williams's 'residual' and 'emergent' (p. 33); 'The custom of workers' control, widely regarded as a right, had become deeply embedded in working class culture' and its defence 'became the major locus of class struggle in the opening decades of the twentieth century' (p. 62). 'The Working Class in Recent Canadian Historical Writing', Acadiensis 7:2 (1978), pp. 116–135, read at pp. 116–117 and 134–135: historians still treat the new study of class 'as little more than interesting additional facts', but 'the new history is well on its way to transforming our understanding of the entire course and structure of Canadian development' (p. 116). 'Labour and Working-Class History in Canada: Prospects in the 1980s', Labour/Le Travailleur 7 (1981), pp. 67–94, read in full: the project 'never excluded the study of unions and labour politics', nor called for history 'simply "written from the bottom up," since it always placed the relationship between classes at the centre of the story' (p. 69); a periodization of 'pre-industrial capitalism to 1850; industrial capitalism, 1850 to the mid-1890s; monopoly capitalism, 1890s to 1929; and crisis and reconstruction, 1930 to the present', offered as 'at best tentative' (p. 74); 'I will certainly stand with scholars such as Thompson and Williams who have argued persuasively for the materiality of culture itself' (p. 85); class 'does have an "objective" side', but '"Class-for-itself," or the failure of the working class to develop such, is almost by definition what working-class history concerns itself with' (pp. 85–86); work on the 1880s found 'a class surprisingly united', in which divisions 'of ethnicity, skill, religion, and even sex were recognized, debated, and for a few years in the 1880s, at least, were overcome', and 'it is now necessary to locate class conflict and class struggle at the centre of modern Canadian history' (p. 89). He places himself among scholars who were 'active in the new left and influenced by the rebirth of Marxist scholarship' (p. 93). Toronto Workers (1980) is unread; Brody quotes its introduction: 'The work will have succeeded to the extent that it provides convincing evidence that the working class was not just "made" but rather was the result of a dialectical interplay of class forces in which it was one of the actors' (p. xviii, as quoted). In-period critics. David Bercuson, in the same issue (pp. 95–96, read), quotes the 1976 Essays definition of the new labour history and notes that 'Kealey's study of Toronto workers contains at least five chapters devoted to working-class and trade-union politics'; his wider objections are recorded under wcreq_bercuson_1981 and edge_919. David Brody, review, Labour/Le Travailleur 8/9 (1981–82), pp. 361–364, read in full: 'Kealey thus lays the foundation, hitherto largely lacking, for a history of the Toronto labour movement' (p. 362), but 'It is in the interpretation of this information that the book founders'; 'Every strike signifies "class conflict," every labour involvement in public life "class politics"' (p. 363); 'Having overreached himself, he has produced only a useable one' (p. 364). Ian McKay, 'Historians, Anthropology, and the Concept of Culture', Labour/Le Travailleur 8/9 (1981–82), cites Kealey's 1981 'defence of the term' (p. 214 n. 88) and argues that working-class culture has 'weak explanatory value' and that Williams's residual and emergent categories 'merely have allowed social historians to indulge in retrospective cheerleading for progressive ideas' (p. 223 and n. 122); Kealey in 1981 called McKay's unpublished paper 'one of the most substantive critiques of Thompson and culturalism' (p. 91 n.). Bettina Bradbury (1987, pp. 35–36, read) and Joan Sangster (2000, p. 133, read): see edge pe138_kealey_rel_05 and the node; Sangster: 'One of the first major collections of the new labour history contained not one article on women' (p. 133, of Kealey and Warrian's Essays, 1976). Desmond Morton (2000, pp. 23–24, read): 'some of the Kealey-Palmer claims for their "new" history were challenged'; 'If, as Kealey insisted, Toronto's working class achieved unity across ethnic and sectarian barriers, it must have been for the briefest of moments in the city contemporaries sometimes called "the Belfast of North America"'. A contribution, not a founding: Freeman (2002) names him in the founding generation of Labour/Le Travail; he presents the work as 'conceived collectively' (1981, p. 68 n. 8). Scope: this edge is Kealey's own contribution; edge_919 carries Palmer's craft culture, edge_886 and edge_890 the Marxist and Thompsonian resources. The Knights of Labor book (1982) is unread and appears in pe138_kealey_rel_05.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: class_culture_community ('The new labour history: class, culture and community'; works Palmer 1979, 1983; Kealey 1980; Kealey and Palmer 1982) already lists him. The 1981 programme also belongs to culture_debate_1981, whose focus calls the essay a 'reply' (see proposed_text_revisions).

proposed_edges.relationship: Limited identities and regional explanation criticised from a class standpoint: 'limited identities' as 'neither "limited" nor analytically separable' (1978), region as 'the crucial variable' 'increasingly misplaced' and western exceptionalism overstated (1981), and the 1919 revolt as 'national in character' (1984)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words, in period. Acadiensis 7:2 (1978), read at pp. 116–117 and 134–135: Cook and Careless 'called for a turn away from nation and politics' toward 'region, ethnicity and class' (p. 116, citing Cook 1967 and Careless 1969); 'The call for attention to "limited identities" was the death-knell of Laurentianism' (p. 117); 'The long-overdue insertion of a class analysis into Canadian historical writing already promises overviews which transcend the refreshing and liberating pluralism of the 1960s calls for attention to region, ethnicity and class. It should be increasingly clear, however, that these so-called "limited identities" are neither "limited" nor analytically separable. No historical notion of class (and there can be no other useful notion) can fail to incorporate ethnicity and place' (p. 135). Labour/Le Travailleur 7 (1981), read in full: 'NONE CAN DENY the importance of regional differences … Yet the increasing emphasis placed on "region" as the crucial variable which explains sundry problems of Canadian development seems increasingly misplaced', citing Westfall on the regional interpretation standing 'the old nationalist history on its head' (p. 74); before the 1890s 'there was not one Canadian working class but many' (p. 75); accounts of western workers are shaped by 'a strong sense of western exceptionalism', and 'the rather easy assumptions of a unique western working-class militancy have been overstated', with n. 25: 'David Bercuson has been most guilty of this' (p. 76); 'Canadian historians have come to believe everything was different everywhere … This celebration of region has fit very well with the general direction of Canadian political life in the last decade. Surely the time has come to begin to reflect on region in a critical way' (p. 76); his remedy is not 'A return to an old national history? No, of course not, but rather the consideration on a national scale of the particular class experiences of Canadian workers in local and regional contexts which adds up to something more than local and regional exceptionalism' (p. 77). '1919: The Canadian Labour Revolt', Labour/Le Travail 13 (1984), pp. 11–44, read at pp. 11–17: 'These examples are intended simply to demonstrate that the revolt was national in character and that its seeds were not rooted in any unique regional fermentation. The "radical" west and the conservative east have become sorry shibboleths of Canadian historiography'; 'the similarities of struggle begin to outweigh the initial impression of regional particularism' (p. 15). Qualifications kept: he grants 'the importance of regional differences' (1981, p. 74) and calls Maritime underdevelopment real (pp. 75–76); the 1978 sentence welcomes the 1960s pluralism as 'refreshing and liberating' before arguing that class analysis transcends it. In-period reading: Morton (2000, p. 25, read) credits Kealey, Palmer, Heron, Hann and others with bringing labour history 'back from superstructure, politics, and the exceptionalism of Western Canada to regions that had been largely neglected by their predecessors: Ontario and the Maritimes'. No reply by Bercuson to the 1981 or 1984 regional argument was checked. Distinct from Cook's 1977–83 critique of regionalism (edge from ramsay_cook to cdn_regional), which doubts region as a unit; Kealey's subordinates it to class and national-scale capitalism.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: limited_identities holds Cook's phrase and Careless's programme, the position the 1978 essay names. The 1981 and 1984 arguments against western exceptionalism also bear on prairie_west; questioning_region (2000 critiques) is the alternative address.

proposed_edges.relationship: Herbert Gutman's cultural history of American workers and David Montgomery's workers' control as models for Kealey's Toronto studies (1976–81), as Kealey and his reviewers said, with the criticisms of Gutman he reported and Brody's verdict that he did not follow Gutman's method
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own statements. 1976 (Labour/Le Travailleur 1, read at pp. 32–34, 58): 'David Montgomery has suggested that we must look beyond pre-industrial cultural forms if we are to understand the behaviour of skilled workers', who were 'veterans of industrial life' (p. 33); on the meaning of shop-floor power, 'David Montgomery has argued that the major impact of this early workers' control was the skilled workers' growing awareness that the key institution for the transformation of society was the trade union' (p. 58). 1978 (Acadiensis, p. 117): the works of Thompson and Hobsbawm, 'and later of Americans such as Herbert Gutman and David Montgomery, had their effects in Canada on a new generation of graduate students'. 1981 (Labour/Le Travailleur 7, read in full): 'A cultural approach in American work on labour history also generated a significant breakthrough. Most notably associated with Herbert Gutman' (p. 81); n. 33: 'Gutman's influence can be seen in numerous recent studies. In Canada see Palmer, A Culture in Conflict and Kealey, Toronto Workers' (p. 82). He reports Dubofsky's and Montgomery's worry about 'the failure to consider the political and economic context' and Brody's charge that Gutman 'shifted the Thompsonian focus on class and culture into a focus solely on culture' (pp. 81–82). In-period readers. David Brody (Labour/Le Travailleur 8/9, 1981–82, read): 'During his tenure at Rochester a decade or so ago, Herbert G. Gutman built up a remarkable graduate program in American working-class history … Gregory Kealey's book bears the marks of what might be termed the Gutman school' (p. 361); but 'In one crucial way, unfortunately, it does not': Gutman 'invariably has drawn his ideas out from the evidence', and 'Had he adhered to the prudent craft of his mentor, Kealey might have written a powerful book' (p. 364). Morton (2000, pp. 22–23, read): the 'second generation' 'travelled abroad, to Warwick, Rochester, and Binghamton, to meet their American and British mentors', and the Knights of Labor records 'Kealey had been able to study at Rochester'. Later engagement, title level only: 'Herbert G. Gutman, 1928–1985, and the Writing of Working-Class History' (Monthly Review, 1986) and 'Gutman and Montgomery' (ILWCH, 1990; wcreq_kealey_1990). Gutman and Montgomery are historians on the newleft roster (work_cultures strand). Influence, not discipleship: the 1981 essay also gives Thompson and Williams as touchstones, and edge_890 carries Thompson's place in the field. edge_888 (newleft ↔ cdn_working_class) stays as the group-level comparison.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: Target is a person entry (no strands). On the source side the relevant newleft strand is work_cultures (Gutman, Montgomery).

proposed_edges.relationship: State surveillance of labour and the left from the First World War: a 1992 documentary article on the RCMP and the Special Branch, arguing that 'For the RCMP the Cold War began in 1919, not in 1946', and the RCMP Security Bulletins he co-edited with Whitaker (1989–97); the work was announced as under way in 1988, and the later syntheses Secret Service (2012, with Whitaker and Parnaby) and Spying on Canadians (2017) are cited at catalogue level only
proposed_edges.map_label: Political policing: the Cold War from 1919, 1992
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The checked intervention, 1992. 'The RCMP, the Special Branch, and the Early Days of the Communist Party of Canada: A Documentary Article', Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), pp. 169–204, introduction read (pp. 169–171; the documents themselves not read): a 1991 visit to the Public Record Office in London, 'when combined with a number of Access to Information requests to the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS), provides considerable insight into the early co-operation between the fledgling Royal Canadian Mounted Police security and intelligence apparatus of the early 1920s and its more experienced partners in England' (p. 169); the weekly RCMP security bulletin was 'circulated to Cabinet', and the bulletins were 'routinely sent to the Special Branch at the Colonial Office' (p. 170); 'Such documentation also makes clear how early Canadian intelligence efforts focused on labour radicalism and socialism. For the RCMP the Cold War began in 1919, not in 1946' (p. 171). His n. 4 (p. 170) describes 'the multi-volume Gregory S. Kealey and Reg Whitaker, eds., The RCMP Security Bulletins (St. John's 1989 and forthcoming)', drawn 'primarily' from Access requests to CSIS; the edition itself is known only through that note and review records. Earlier notice, not a checked argument: the 1988 author note in Class, Gender, and Region (p. iv, read) says only that he 'is currently working on Canadian state repression of labour and the left'; the 1919 essay (1984, p. 43, read) draws on an RCMP draft memorandum of September 1919. Later works, catalogue level only and not assessed here: 'State Repression of Labour and the Left in Canada, 1914–20' (CHR 73:3, 1992, pp. 281–314) and 'The Surveillance State' (Intelligence and National Security 7:3, 1992, pp. 179–210), both reprinted as chapters of Spying on Canadians (2017; UTP chapter records); Secret Service: Political Policing in Canada from the Fenians to Fortress America (2012), by Reg Whitaker, Gregory S. Kealey and Andrew Parnaby (publisher's description: 'the many tensions that arise when undercover police and their covert methods are deployed too freely in a liberal democratic society'). The edge therefore claims the 1992 argument and the edition, not the content of the later syntheses. Relation to the strand: security_state currently holds Whitaker and Marcuse's Cold War Canada (1945–57). Kealey's argument dates the security state's anti-communist focus to 1919; this is an extension in time by Whitaker's co-editor, not a critique of their book. No in-period reviews of the Bulletins were read (Dansereau, RHAF 1995, located only).
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: security_state ('The Cold War security state'; Whitaker and Marcuse 1994). On acceptance the strand's person_ids and works could add Kealey and Whitaker (1989–97).

proposed_edges.relationship: Co-authors of Dreaming of What Might Be (1982) and allies in the new labour history, read together by critics as 'the Kealey-Palmer claims', though 'differently positioned politically' (Sangster) and with different emphases: workers' control and class analysis for Kealey, craft culture for Palmer
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Collaboration, in their own texts. Kealey's 1976 essay thanks Palmer, with David Frank and Craig Heron, for comments (p. 32 n.); the 1981 essay thanks him among others (p. 94), refers readers to Palmer's forthcoming Making of E.P. Thompson (p. 82), and says that 'Kealey and Palmer, "Dreaming of What Might Be"' 'argues this position at length' on the value of the romantic and utopian traditions, which gave workers 'the ability to dream of an alternative future' (p. 84 and n. 39). Read together by critics, in period. Bercuson (1981, p. 96): 'the Palmer and Kealey books' as 'restricted but intensive studies'. Bradbury (Labour/Le Travail 19, 1987, pp. 35–36, read) quotes Dreaming (p. 318) and writes that to dismiss partially a Knights of Labor editor's picture of a wife who 'can darn a stocking' 'as "offensive" and as "crude moralizing," as Kealey and Palmer do, seems to me both to deny the realities of the division of labour within the working-class family economy at that time, and to close off the possibility of examining this very important element of a skilled worker's pride'; she adds that 'Kealey and Palmer quite rightly point out' that a Montreal workman's statement stopped short of a critique of 'women's proper sphere'. Sangster (Labour/Le Travail 46, 2000, p. 133, read): 'Two seminal studies followed by Gregory Kealey and Bryan Palmer. Though differently positioned politically, they examined workers' responses to 19th century industrialization, with a proclivity to centre on skilled male workers and their actions in the public sphere.' Morton (2000, pp. 23–24, read): 'some of the Kealey-Palmer claims for their "new" history were challenged'; Stanley Ryerson (1981, as Morton reports it) argued that the Knights were 'devoutly committed to labour-employer harmony and industrial peace'. Later reading, labelled: McCoy (2021) quotes their chapter: 'A subordinate class must reach toward an alternative hegemony if it ever hopes to dominate the ethos of society' (Dreaming, p. 277, as quoted). The book itself is unread. A comparison, not an influence: the edge records co-authorship and joint reception. Their different emphases are recorded in edge_919 (Palmer's craft culture) and pe138_kealey_rel_01 (Kealey's workers' control and class analysis).
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: Person-to-person comparison; neither endpoint has strands.

proposed_edges.relationship: Careless's second thoughts about the 'flood' of regional, cultural and class writing (1979 lecture) read as a reaction reasserting 'a "positive" unifying national history' (1988); a decade earlier the working-class bibliography Kealey co-compiled had invoked Careless's limited identities (1973)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Kealey's words, in period. Introduction to Class, Gender, and Region: Essays in Canadian Historical Sociology (St. John's: CCLH, 1988; reprint of a Canadian Journal of Sociology special issue), pp. 1–7, read in the AU Press PDF: 'The degree to which reaction has re-emerged to reassert the need for a "positive" unifying national history can be seen by contrasting the views of J.M.S. Careless in 1969 and in 1980. In 1969, Careless enthusiastically embraced Ramsay Cook's earlier call for the study of region, class, and ethnicity … By 1980, however, he had serious doubts' (p. 2); he quotes Careless's farmer 'in the midst of the flood' and answers: 'As I hope this volume suggests, such plaintiff [sic] Toronto cries to date have not been able to dam the flood of critical scholarship on class, gender, and region' (p. 3). 'The impatience mentioned by Berger and articulated by Careless addresses itself as much to this regional revolt as it does to writings concerned with class and gender' (p. 5). Careless's text, re-read (Manitoba History no. 1, web text, unpaginated; the 1979 Jackson lecture, cited by Kealey as 1980): 'there has been a massive outpouring … on class disparities and stresses and such things as national concerns are by and large passed over or discounted. In this situation, I feel a little like the farmer in the midst of a flood'. Qualifications kept: Careless continues, 'there are reasons why I do not really feel as bad as the foregoing might suggest', calls working-class history 'one of the most active and productive areas' of the study of limited identities, and asks that class identities 'be treated in their national scope', a point close to Kealey's own (1981, p. 77). Kealey's 'reaction' is his reading of the lecture. Earlier connection: Careless (1979) quotes the introduction to Primary Sources in Canadian Working-Class History (1973, p. 11), compiled by Hann, Gregory and Linda Kealey and Warrian: 'For some time J. M. S. Careless has called for … a historical appreciation of the varieties of "limited identities" that constitute Canada'. Kealey (1981, p. 68) says that statement was 'drafted by Russell Hann'. No reply by Careless was checked. Related: edge_954 (Careless → who_killed_debate) records the fragmentation worry this passage voices; pe138_kealey_rel_02 records Kealey's separate critique of limited identities from a class standpoint (1978).
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: Target is a person entry (no strands).

proposed_edges.relationship: Ethnic history criticised for treating ethnicity apart from class and for 'official ethnic interpreters' whose celebratory histories leave out working-class militancy, while ethnicity is kept as a subject of cultural analysis (1981)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words, in period: 'Labour and Working-Class History in Canada: Prospects in the 1980s', Labour/Le Travailleur 7 (1981), section III, 'Ethnicity', pp. 77–80, read in full. 'The literature on ethnicity and immigration, even in "multicultural" Canada, too often ignores ethnicity as an ongoing factor in historical analysis. … Instead one might question the official ethnic interpreters of their history where middle class bias and, all too often, cold war assumptions have come to dominate the quasi-official version of the past. This past, which celebrates the achievements of each ethnic community, has little room in its pages for the embarrassments of working-class militancy and radical politics' (p. 78); 'Ethnicity considered independent of class often obscures important issues', with the Italian padrone 'King' Cordasco as an instance of 'important class divisions within the ethnic communities themselves'; 'Here again class will prove more crucial than some ethnic historians have previously suggested' (p. 79). He also notes that labour historians who studied militancy (Bercuson, McCormack, Abella) 'have moved towards ethnicity as a crucial variable for further study' (p. 88). Qualifications kept: 'Concern for the ethnic divisions within the working class then is important and valid' (p. 73); 'This qualification is not meant to diminish the significance of ethnicity and of the potentially divisive nature of ethnic heterogeneity to the Canadian working class' (p. 78); ethnicity 'is one of the major areas which demands a cultural analysis' (p. 77), and 'cultural analysis will be central to this project' (p. 80). He cites Avery's 'Dangerous Foreigners' (1979) and Harney on padronism in his notes (p. 79). Scope: a critique of ethnic history that sets ethnicity apart from class and of community-sponsored celebratory history, not of the immigrant-workers literature (Avery) the entry's workers_radicalism strand holds. Perin's 'Clio as an Ethnic' (1983) in the ethnic_history_debate strand is a separate, later critique; no exchange between them was checked.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: ethnic_history_debate ('Ethnic history and its critics': Perin, Harney, Iacovetta). Optional edge: it rests on one section of one essay.

wcreq_kealey_1981.note: Read in full for the 1.138 Kealey draft in the journal's PDF (https://lltjournal.ca/index.php/llt/article/view/2657; OJS metadata confirms pp. 67–94 and gives Memorial University). Not a reply to Bercuson's essay: p. 68 calls it 'This essay and the following contribution by David Bercuson', and its starred note says 'Both essays were delivered at the McGill Conference, "Class and Culture: Dimensions of Canada's Labour Past," 7-8 March 1980', revised 'extensively'. It answers Bercuson's 1979 charge of 'obeisance to E.P. Thompson, the guru' (p. 87). Further passages: the project 'always placed the relationship between classes at the centre of the story' (p. 69); the four-stage periodization (p. 74); region 'increasingly misplaced' as 'the crucial variable', 'western exceptionalism', n. 25 'David Bercuson has been most guilty of this', 'everything was different everywhere' (pp. 74–77); ethnicity and 'the official ethnic interpreters' (pp. 77–80); Gutman's influence on Palmer's and Kealey's books (p. 82 n. 33); 'the materiality of culture itself' (p. 85); 'Class-for-itself' (p. 86); 'it is now necessary to locate class conflict and class struggle at the centre of modern Canadian history' (p. 89); McKay's unpublished paper 'one of the most substantive critiques of Thompson and culturalism' (p. 91 n.); the 1970s cohort 'active in the new left and influenced by the rebirth of Marxist scholarship' (p. 93).
